content.comment_body: Hello, I am seeking clarification on the difference between [product_name] and [product_name] Slave in a network project. My understanding is that the [product_name] slave does not necessarily need its own program, although it can have one. Is there any additional information about this? Currently, I have four [product_name] devices configured as [product_name] [version_no] in the network, and they all seem to be operating as Masters. They communicate with each other and with a panel device using S7 communication; some act as servers while others as clients, which was automatically configured by the software and cannot be changed now. I am unsure if this setup is correct. What is the recommended practice for determining which device should be a server or a client in S7 communication? Thank you for your feedback!

The key distinction is that a [product_name] slave operates without a user program, whereas a [product_name] master utilizes the I/O of the slave. Masters can exchange data using S7 communication, allowing you to configure one [product_name] (master) as clients and the others as servers. In your setup, you could create three S7 client connections on one device, and assign the other three devices as S7 servers. In this arrangement, all four [product_name] devices are considered 'masters.'

There are two types of communication for [product_name] S7 connections: 1) Master/slave communication, where one device is set as master and the other as slave, with the slave not running its own program and providing hardware resources to the master; and 2) Client/server connections, where one device is the client and the other the server—here, both devices have their own programs. The client determines what data is sent or received, and device roles are defined during connection setup. There are several methods available to create such connections.
Thank you for the clarifications—this explanation makes things much clearer.
